study.title: Modulatory effects of acupuncture on raphe nucleus-related brain circuits in patients with chronic neck pain: A randomized neuroimaging trial
study.randomization: Block randomization using random number table; independent staff generated random number and grouping scheme using SPSS software (version 20.0; IBM Corp.) with block length and number of segments set to nine according to the block and the number of segments to 11 according to the block randomization principle
study.blinding: Patients blinded to group assignments; acupuncturists not blinded (due to nature of interventions); outcome assessors, data collectors, and statisticians blinded to treatment allocation
study.population: Patients with chronic neck pain recruited from acupuncture and orthopedic clinics at Hospital of Chengdu University of Traditional Chinese Medicine
study.inclusion_criteria: (1) 18–65 years old men or women with neck pain and discomfort or limited cervical motion as the main symptoms; (2) right-hand dominance; (3) pain score of ≥4 cm on the Visual Analog Scale (VAS) for 5 of 7 days (range, 0–10 cm); (4) more than 3 months duration of disease; and (5) informed consent signed by patients
study.exclusion_criteria: (1) macroscopic T2-visible brain lesions on the MRI scans; (2) accompanied by other serious organic lesions, including malignant neoplasms, tuberculosis, fracture, or osteomyelitis; (3) complications associated with serious primary diseases, including cardiovascular, cerebrovascular, liver, kidney, and hematopoietic systems; (4) mental disorders and other mental disorders that could not be matched with the questionnaire (a score of self-rating anxiety scale [SAS] or self-rating depression scale [SDS] > 72); (5) bleeding tendencies, allergies, and skin diseases; pregnancy, lactation, or fertility issues within the past 6 months; (6) contraindications such as metals in the body; and (7) participation in other simultaneous clinical trials

interventions.needle_size_exact: 25–40 mm in length and 0.25–0.30 mm in diameter
interventions.manipulation_exact: Rotating or lifting–thrusting manipulation was performed for Deqi sensation after needle insertion
interventions.deqi_intended_exact: Yes; Deqi sensation (a sensation of soreness, numbness, distention, or radiation that indicated effective needling) intended
interventions.number_of_sessions_exact: 12 sessions total (3 times weekly for 4 weeks)

extraction_notes.note: No quantitative deqi/sensory scale data (e.g., MASS, Southampton Needle Sensation Questionnaire) were reported. Only narrative descriptions of intended and non-intended Deqi were provided.
Expectancy, credibility, and blinding success were not assessed or reported. No instrument was administered for these constructs.

Coordinate space (MNI or Talairach) was not explicitly stated. The paper normalized to an EPI template but did not specify which coordinate space the results are reported in. No MNI or Talairach coordinates were provided in result tables; only region names and atlas labels were given.

No peak or cluster coordinates (x, y, z) were provided for any neuroimaging results. Results are reported as brain region labels only (e.g., LING.L, THA.R) with FC mean ± SD values and ANCOVA p-values.
Smoothing kernel was not reported in the neuroimaging methods section.
Table 1 lists SAS baseline for SA group as 45.83 (9.88), identical to TA group. Table 2 lists SAS baseline for SA group as 43.58 (11.49). This discrepancy is present in the paper itself.

The abstract states 'increased functional connectivity (FC) between the DR and thalamus, between the MR and parahippocampal gyrus, amygdala, and insula' but the neuroimaging outcomes table (Table 3) shows that MR–INS.L and MR–INS.R and MR–PHG.L changes in TA group are negative (decreased FC). The abstract may be describing the direction of the interaction effect or directionality relative to SA. Caution is warranted in interpreting 'increased' vs 'decreased' FC for the MR–limbic regions.

Figure 4 shows brain slices with highlighted regions for ANCOVA interaction effects, and Figure 5 shows a schematic of raphe nucleus-related circuits. No numerical coordinates can be extracted from these figures based on the PDF. Coordinates are not readable from the figure.

The paper describes TA as showing 'increased FC between the DR and thalamus' in abstract and discussion, but Table 3 shows TA had treatment-baseline difference of −0.05 (−0.11 to 0.005) for DR_THA.R (decreased), while SA had +0.08. The interaction (pT*G = 0.0009) is significant with opposing directions. The TA 'increased' relative to SA direction is likely the intended interpretation but the TA group's own within-subject change is a decrease.

The paper's description of 'reconfiguration' of TA in Figure 5 uses yellow lines for 'TA increased FC' and blue lines for 'TA decreased FC'. Based on text, TA increased FC: DR–thalamus (relative to SA), MR–amygdala, MR–insula, MR–parahippocampal gyrus; TA decreased FC: DR–lingual gyrus, DR–middle frontal gyrus (left), MR–middle frontal gyrus (right). However, absolute within-group changes differ from this framing (see previous note).
Cluster sizes (in voxels or mm3) were not reported in Table 3. Only mean ± SD FC values and p-values were tabulated.

The seed coordinates for DR (0, −27, −9) and MR (0, −31, −21) are cited from reference [27] in the text (Blanpied et al. 2017, which is a clinical neck pain guideline). This is likely a citation error in the paper and the actual coordinate source is references [42] and [43] (Beliveau et al. 2015; Han et al. 2019) which are the PET/fMRI studies described in the methods section. Coordinates were extracted exactly as reported.

Duration of illness baseline data (months) are reported in Table 1 for TA (83.14 ± 60.49) and SA (96.96 ± 94.75) but are not extracted as a clinical outcome because they were not assessed as a treatment outcome measure.
The paper mentions 'run-in period' of 2 weeks before randomization but does not report data collected during this period.

The 2:1 randomization ratio resulted in TA=66 and SA=33. References [28-31] cited for this design ratio relate to neurological drug trials; the clinical rationale for this unequal allocation in an acupuncture trial is not fully elaborated.
